As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the tariff schedules do not reveal the actual protection afforded by the tariff because of the operation of the special or Anti-dumping Duty Act. To my mind the special or Anti-dumping Duty Act may properly be regarded as the most wicked piece of legislation on the statute books to-day, and it is significant that this government have made no attempt to restrict its power, but have sought rather to enlarge its operation. This special act has been invoked 4,888 times during the past two years, according to a return tabled in this House a few days ago; so it is quite evident the large part it plays in the protection game as played in this country.
Now then, Mr. Speaker, if the facts are as I have stated and the amount of protection afforded foy the tariff is really greater to-day than it was in 1921, we are confronted by a most remarkable situation. In the first place, there is the fact that approximately 115 members supporting the government were elected on a platform the chief planks of which emphasized the desirability of reduced tariffs. But that is not all; for in addition to the 115 there were another sixty members elected to this House who were more or less pledged to work for a reduction of tariff. This makes a total of perhaps 160 or

The Budget-Mr. McTaggart
170 members who comprise what we should call the low tariff forces in this House, out of a total membership of 235; and notwithstanding this preponderance of low tariff views the tariff continues to grow higher amd higher in every way. This very extraordinary situation has been the subject of considerable thought on my part, Mr. Speaker, and prompted me to an analysis of my own vote on previous budgets. I find that on two occasions in the life of this parliament I voted confidence in the government's promise to reduce tariffs; but if appearances be not too deceiving I am prepared to admit that perhaps I may have been flimflammed.
In all seriousness, I should like to ask: if this parliament, made up as it is of a membership three quarters of which may be expected to favour lower tariffs, can make no more progress along this line than we have done during the last three years, what is the future? This year a crown sheet is being placed in the protectionist armour of the tariff in the shape of a tariff commission, so it is abundantly apparent that this government is definitely wedded to the principle of protection. Members to the right have been making a lot of noise over the fact that a number of industries have closed their doors, and seem wholly unconscious of the fact that with increased protection there must follow decreased purchasing power and consequently more closed factories.
Then again, Mr. Speaker, members on the right tefll us we should have more consideration for our own workmen than those -abroad, and the way they ask us to show that -consideration is by bringing the workmen from abroad to our shores. Reverting to the Wtays and Means resolutions of the budget, Mr. Speaker, allow me to voice very strong objection to the amendment to the Special War Revenue Act 1915 defining the meaning of the word cheque:
That " cheque " shall be further defined to include any document or writing, not drawn upon or addressed

to a bank, in exchange for which a bank makes payment of a sum of money, except a coupon and a document used solely for the purpose of settling or clearing any account between banks, and that such a cheque shall be liable to the stamp tax imposed on cheques by the said act.
If this amendment be accepted by parliament it will mean that all coupons including cream checks and grain -checks will be liable to the fax. In the case of grain checks the abjection may not be as great, taking into account the need for revenue and the further fact that grain checks, or -tickets as they are sometimes called, are usually for considerable amounts. But in the case of cream tickets, which are usuallly for small amounts, I feel that the government would be well advised to provide for their exemption on amounts under ten doJlars. If the tax be allowed to stand it is bound to have the effect of checking and discouraging the system of mixed farming which has been making fairly satisfactory progress in the prairie provinces during the last few years.

Now I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the financial journals of this country should be able to interpret the financial statement if anyone in the country could, but it is very evident that the Times has been unable to do so with any degree of accuracy. I think the fact has been established, however, that the
nation's obligations are heavier to-day than a year ago by an amount anywhere between sixty and one hundred and thirty millions of dollars, but no hint of this somewhat alarming situation is revealed in the budget. The significance of this situation should be of deep interest to the general public, but it may be that the general public will be too busy rejoicing over the 52 millions saved in taxes, as announced in the screaming head-lines in the party press, to get down to sober reflection on the unsatisfactory state of the nation's balance-sheet. It may be that the government are not wholly to blame for the unsatisfactory state of the country's finances, but at any rate it would seem to me that they are to blame for their failure to reveal what the true situation is at the present time.
But what of the future Mr. Speaker? How much longer may we expect that even the most capable of finance ministers shall be able to cope successfully with the problem of an unbalanced budget? And I wonder how many cunning new tax schemes may be added to the already overburdened consumer ere the breaking point is reached? We are all familiar with the tax on imports with its resultant restriction of trade; but this year another method of restricting trade is being thrust forward as a panacea for some of our economic ills:	Not satisfied with a tax on
imports to make the cost of goods higher to the consumer, we now propose to place a tax on exports so that the goods which the producer has to sell may be placed under a further handicap in the markets of the world. The present budget contemplates an export tax on power, and this I do not propose to criticize as I am not familiar with the question, but I am interested in the suggested tax on wheat. To my mind such a tax would have the effect of seriously restricting the market for Canadian wheat, with a consequent depression of prices, and would not accomplish the prevention of mixing in transit as carried on at the present time.
The trouble with nearly all of the tax schemes which are so popular with the government of the day is that in the final analysis they are carried almost wholly by the farmers and working classes, and those classes of our people are now carrying almost the maximum load which they are able to bear. But however unpopular with the masses of the people the imposition of taxes may be we must have a large annual revenue to take care of the expenses of government as well as our obligations to the bond-holding classes who grew fat during the war period. Why close our eyes

The Budget-Mr. McTaggart
to the fact that during the war period the government's failure to adequately tax the profits derived as a result of the war had the effect of transferring to the bond-holding classes almost complete ownership and control of the implements of production? Might it not be appropriate at this time to ask how much longer the Minister of Finance can afford to ignore our billion dollars of tax-free bonds as a possible avenue of taxation? Is it not about time that we in Canada woke up to the fact that the bond-holding classes are not paying their proportionate share of the tax burden of the country? I think I recognize the difficulty which is sure to be encountered if an attempt were made to institute a levy on the tax-free bonds, but I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in these days of B.N.A. uncertainties it is doubtful if the government possessed the right to make those bonds tax-free.
At any rate Mr. Speaker, for my part, I feel quite convinced that our finance minister, or his successor, whoever he may be, must of necessity adopt one of three alternatives in his search for the necessary revenue to conduct the affairs of the country: he must increase the load on the consumer and take chances; impose some form of capital levy and take no chances; or failing this, he may be forced to the historic expedient of despairing finance ministers and inflate the currency. Now I hope, Mr. Speaker, no one will rise to accuse me of belonging to that antiquated school of thought which sees in inflation of the currency the solution of all our economic ills. I am in favour of a stabilized currency and the uniform price-level, but at the same time I am not unconscious of the fact that under present arrangements the control of the currency reposes mainly in the hands of the Minister of Finance, and I am just a bit frightened that some day he may be reduced to that attitude of despair of meeting the country's obligations, which may prompt him to resort to methods which he would be the first to decry to-day. I appreciate the ridicule which such a suggestion is sure to meet in this House at this time, but I should like to point out that inflation of the currency is becoming quite a popular topic among many of our people to-day.
We have heard not a little in this House during the last two years in regard to the control of credit, and I have noted with satisfaction that the minister has consistently refused to be impressed, but it would indeed be a cold and cheerless irony if the minister were at last compelled to adopt the ex-

pedient which he has frowned upon so diligently.
We all recognize the fact that inflation is simply a tax on the creditor or bondholding classes in any country, but surely such an alternative would not need to be resorted to in Canada, with all its unfortunate consequences, if the bondholders could be made to see the fairness and justice of a modified form of capital levy.
We have heard something in this House about the prosperity at present enjoyed by France, and this so-called prosperity has been ascribed to the system of protection in vogue there. Well, Mr. Speaker, I submit that if France has protection it can hardly be on a very extensive scale, for she has not protected her currency and she does not propose to protect- her bondholders. The Bank of P'rance, with the approval of the government, recently inflated the currency to the extent of two billion francs, and only a few days ago the government of France met with defeat in their attempt to impose the capital levy.
I hold in my hand a copy of a dsspatch from a Paris newspaper to the Toronto Globe, part of which reads as follows:
We must know if henceforth the bank note of the Bank of France is worthy of public confidence, it declares. If we can no longer believe in the loyalty, sincerity and honesty of the statements of the Bank of France, how can we trust its bank note? This is the first time in our history that the government has put into circulation illegal money, and the first time the Bank of France hid this crime by fraudulent statements. If such acts remain unpunished the credit of the Bank of France is finished.
Now, Mr. Speaker, my point is this: The situation in France is somewhat similar to the situation in Canada, in that both countries are enveloped in debt; and the Finance Minister in France was driven to the expedient of inflating the currency in a heroic effort to present a balanced budget. In Canada we have not yet reached the point where such drastic expedients may be necessary, but let us hope that our Finance Minister may scrutinize closely the urgency and wisdom of a moderate tax on capital. I should like to leave these thoughts with the Finance Minister and to express the hope that he may not discard them as being the meaningless mouth-ings of a calamity howler. I am not afraid of the future so far as Canada is concerned, if we can only cut out the political clap-trap and get down to the business of placing the country on its feet. But to stand complacently aboard a sinking ship and shout ''calamity howler!" at the forces who are manning the pumps is not the kind of philosophy W'hich should be popular at this time.
